title: A US Trade Delegation Is Coming to Delhi on June 1. The Full Bilateral Trade Agreement Is on the Table. Here Is What NRI Investors Need to Watch.
excerpt: The interim deal cut tariffs to 18 per cent. The next round of talks aims to lock in market access, customs facilitation, and digital trade rules. For NRIs with money on both sides of the Pacific, the details will decide whether your portfolio tilts east or west.
body:
The interim deal is signed. The tariffs are down from 26 to 18 per cent. And now the real negotiation begins.

A US trade delegation led by the Chief Negotiator for the Bilateral Trade Agreement will arrive in New Delhi on June 1 for four days of talks that will shape the economic relationship between the world's largest economy and the world's most populous democracy for the next decade. The discussions will cover five areas: market access, non-tariff measures, customs facilitation, investment promotion, and economic security.

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans — and the millions more with investments, family businesses, and property on both sides — this round of talks is not abstract policy. It is a direct line to your portfolio, your remittances, and your parents' retirement.

Where Things Stand

The February 2026 interim agreement was a handshake, not a marriage. The US reduced reciprocal tariffs on Indian goods from 26 to 18 per cent. India agreed to lower tariffs on US industrial goods — from an average of 13.5 per cent toward zero — and opened its agriculture sector to a wide range of American products, with zero duties on tree nuts, wine, spirits, fruits, and vegetables.

But the deal left critical issues on the table. Digital trade rules — covering data localisation, cross-border data flows, and platform regulation — were explicitly deferred. Dairy and "sensitive" agricultural items were excluded. India committed to purchasing $100 billion worth of US products annually for five years, largely aircraft, technology, precious metals, oil, nuclear products, and agricultural goods, but the joint statement formalising the deal is still being drafted.

US Ambassador Sergio Gor said on May 21 that the full BTA could be finalised in "coming weeks and months" — a timeline that would be historic. The EU-India FTA, signed in January 2026, took 19 years to negotiate. The US is trying to do it in 18 months.

What Rubio's Visit Revealed

Secretary of State Marco Rubio's four-day India visit last week — his first as both Secretary of State and National Security Advisor — previewed the pressure points. Energy was the headline. Washington wants India to buy more American oil and gas, particularly as the Iran conflict has disrupted traditional supply routes through the Strait of Hormuz and oil has climbed back above $94 a barrel.

India, the world's second-largest oil importer, has been diversifying away from Iranian and Russian crude under US pressure. The interim deal reportedly included a commitment to $500 billion in US energy, technology, agricultural, coal, and other products — a number Trump announced on Truth Social and Modi partially confirmed.

But the Quad meeting in India also surfaced tensions. Rubio framed trade friction as a feature of America First, not a bug: "This is not about India, it's about the United States in terms of trade." For Indian negotiators, the message was clear — concessions on agriculture and energy are the price of access to the American market.

What NRI Investors Should Watch

IT and services: The full BTA is expected to address services trade — the area where India runs a massive surplus. Any provisions on H-1B visa pathways, digital services taxation, or data localisation rules will directly affect Indian IT companies and the NRIs who work for them. Watch for language on cross-border data flows.

Agriculture and FMCG: India has protected dairy, GM products, soya meal, poultry, maize, and corn. If any of these open up in the full deal, Indian agribusiness stocks will move. Companies like ITC, Nestlé India, and Britannia are directly exposed.

Energy and defence: The $500 billion commitment tilts heavily toward US energy imports. Indian refiners like Reliance Industries and BPCL are already adjusting supply chains. Defence procurement from US manufacturers could accelerate, benefiting L&T Defence and Bharat Electronics.

The rupee: The bilateral trade deficit — India exported $87 billion to the US in FY25 while importing $45 billion — is under scrutiny. Any deal that substantially increases Indian imports of US goods will put pressure on the rupee, which has already hit all-time lows near 95.69 against the dollar.

Pharma: India's generic drug industry has been conspicuously absent from deal announcements. The US is India's largest pharma export market. Any new intellectual property provisions in the BTA could reshape the generics landscape.

The Bottom Line

The June 1-4 talks are the most consequential round of US-India economic negotiations since the nuclear deal of 2008. The interim agreement proved both sides can move fast. The question is whether the full deal can satisfy a White House that wants to "open up India" and a New Delhi that needs to protect farmers, dairy producers, and domestic manufacturing.

For NRI investors, the playbook is straightforward: watch the joint statement, read the fine print on agriculture and digital trade, and hedge your rupee exposure. The deal that emerges from these talks will determine whether the $500 billion bilateral trade target is an aspiration or an inevitability.

Ambassador Gor was characteristically diplomatic: the deal will "strengthen supply chains and drive sustained inclusive growth." What he did not say is that someone has to pay for inclusion, and the negotiation over who that is starts on June 1.
author: Diaspora Desk
